1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5.name: Latvian Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5.background: Analysed by Giulio Cesare Polerio in the late sixteenth century, it came to be called the Greco Countergambit after Gioachino Greco. Its present name honours several Latvian players who analysed it, most prominently Kārlis Bētiņš.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5.strategy: The principal reply: White takes the undefended pawn, and with the knight on e5 the check on h5 becomes a real threat, since ...g6 would simply lose to Nxg6. Black must challenge the knight before taking on e4, so White starts with an extra pawn and the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.strategy: Accepts the gambit and keeps the pawn. Black kicks the knight with ...e4 and plays for quick development, so White must spend time on the knight and look after the extra pawn. Sound, but it gives Black more play than Nxe5, which wins a pawn and keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4.name: Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4.background: Carl Mayet, a Berlin master, reached this position in 1837, by the move order 2.Bc4 and 3.Nf3.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops towards f7 but lets Black take on e4: after Nxe5 the pawns are level, and ...d5 hits the bishop and gives Black a strong centre. The play stays very sharp, but White has traded the extra pawn that 3.Nxe5 wins for an equal fight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.d4.name: Latvian Gambit: Mason Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.d4.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, but gives up the edge that Nxe5 wins: after ...fxe4 the knight on f3 is attacked and the best White gets is level material. The play turns sharp, with White often sacrificing a piece, but Black has adequate defences, so it brings complications rather than an advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nc3.name: Latvian Gambit: Mlotkowski Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nc3.background: The American master Stasch Mlotkowski (1881–1943) originally analysed it, in the 1916 British Chess Magazine.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and meets ...fxe4 by taking on e5 rather than recapturing on e4, where Black would get ...d5 and a big centre. A quiet way to decline the gambit, but it lets Black choose the structure, and Black's best reply gives a strong centre and good bishops.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.c4.name: Latvian Gambit: Diepstraten Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.c4.strategy: A slow queenside move that develops no piece and does nothing about the pawn on f5. It also sets a trap for White itself: after ...fxe4 and Nxe5, ...Nf6 and ...d6 catch the knight if White pushes d4 carelessly.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.g4.name: Latvian Gambit: Lobster Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.g4.strategy: A reckless pawn thrust that weakens the whole kingside. White hopes Black will grab the pawn, but taking the centre pawn with ...fxe4 instead hits the knight, and after Nxe5 ...d6 drives it away again, leaving White with the worse game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.b4.name: Latvian Gambit: Senechaud Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.b4.strategy: Sets a trap for the greedy: after ...fxe4 and Nxe5, taking the pawn with ...Bxb4 runs into Qh5+ and Nxg6, and White ends up winning the rook on h8. If Black declines and simply develops, the wing pawn move has done nothing for the centre or development, and Black stands better.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4.strategy: Black takes the pawn the gambit was played for. White can take back on e5, so material is level at once, but the game is sharp, with the bishop and knight aimed at f7 and Black's king short of cover. Declining would leave White a free hand.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 Nf6.name: Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack, Morgado Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 Nf6.background: The most common amateur reply to the Mayet Attack, usually played by people used to the Latvian Gambit Accepted.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and covers h5, but leaves the pawn on e5 to be taken while the bishop already aims at f7. After Nxe5 and ...fxe4, the knight jump to f7 forks queen and rook. Black is walking into a line that costs material.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 b5.name: Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack, Strautins Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 b5.strategy: Rare and dubious: it tries to deflect the bishop from its diagonal towards f7, but Bxb5 simply wins a pawn, and Black still has to solve the problem of the exposed kingside.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5.strategy: The only move that makes sense: White regains the pawn and threatens a knight jump to f7, forking queen and rook, because the bishop on c4 guards f7 and the king cannot take.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Bxg8.strategy: Wins the knight on g8, but ...exf3 takes White's knight in return and leaves the bishop on g8 attacked by the rook on h8. White can save the bishop only by giving up a pawn or more, and Black's pieces are the more active.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Ng5.strategy: Hangs the knight: ...Qxg5 takes it for nothing. The knight eyes e4 and f7, but the queen on d8 sees g5 along the diagonal, so the attack never happens.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 d5.name: Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack, Polerio-Svedenborg Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 d5.background: Known as the Polerio-Svedenborg Variation, it is by far the most common fourth move for Black in the Mayet Attack. The Latvian Gambit specialists Kon Grivainis and John Elburg report that Black wins more often than White in this line.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 d5.strategy: Meets the threat on f7 directly: the pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal, hits the bishop and supports the pawn on e4. Black gets a strong centre in return for an exposed kingside, which makes this the accurate way to defend.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5.strategy: Hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once and sets a trap: the tempting Nf7 lets Black take on g2 with a dangerous attack. White simply answers with a pawn in the centre, and Black is left gambling on a poisoned pawn with the queen far from home.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6.name: Latvian Gambit: Corkscrew Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hopes for the knight jump to f7, answered by ...Qe7, so that Black traps the knight on h8 and attacks the king. Accurate play defuses it: White is left a rook up and has to meet a speculative attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6 5.strategy: Forks queen and rook, and the bishop on c4 guards the knight, so the king cannot take it. Black has to give up the rook on h8 and hopes for an attack to compensate, but White can calmly collect the material.

Forces ...Ke7, which blocks the f8-bishop and costs Black the right to castle, and the knight on e5 guards the bishop. Sound and safe, but White wins no material and gives up the fork on f7 that wins the exchange, so the edge is smaller.
Develops with an attack on the pawn on e4, but White gives up the winning fork on f7: ...d5 shuts the bishop out, hits it and defends e4. Black gets a strong centre and the game is level.

Moves the queen out of the fork with a counterattack on the knight, and gives up the rook on h8 for quick development. The knight that takes it will be stuck in the corner, and Black hopes to trap it and pile up against the king in the centre.
Saves the rook but leaves the queen on d8: Nxd8 wins it, and Black's king recaptures only a knight. A fork must be met by moving the more valuable piece, not the lesser one.
Hits the bishop on c4 and ignores the fork: Nxd8 wins the queen for a piece. Black's counterattack on the bishop wins back only a minor piece, not the queen.

Takes the rook. The knight is stranded in the corner, but White is a rook up for now and can give some of it back to escape if Black's pieces become dangerous; calm development is all the position asks.

Retreats the knight and passes up the rook that was there for the taking. White has nothing to show for the trip to f7, while Black has the pawn on e4 and the time to develop, and the knight can be chased by a pawn at once.
Gives the knight away: the check forks king and bishop, but Black takes the knight with the c-pawn or the queen and the fork is gone. White has nothing left for the piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6 5.name: Latvian Gambit: Corkscrew Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6 5.strategy: Black's thematic try: the pawn opens the c8-bishop, hits the bishop on c4 and prepares ...Bg4 against the queen, hoping the knight stuck on h8 and the king in the centre give real chances. It is the best practical try, though White must still develop with care to stay a rook up.

Brings the queenside knight into play and covers d4 and e5, keeping the pawn thrust in reserve. It is slower than the immediate pawn move: the knight on h8 can step out, White gets time to consolidate, and Black remains a rook down.
Takes g6 from the knight in the corner, but the knight steps out to f7, where the bishop guards it, so nothing is trapped. Black has spent a move on a half-measure and is still a rook down.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5.strategy: The real test of the queen's sortie: the pawn opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against the queen and builds a centre. White accepts the loss of g2 for a lead in development, and the game becomes a tactical melee with Black's queen far from home.

Looks like it wins the exchange with a fork, but the queen escapes by taking g2 with tempo on the rook on h1, and White has to save material at once. The knight stays offside while Black develops with an attack.

Keeps the knight on a square the queen on d1 guards and blocks the g-file, so g2 no longer hangs. It hands back the advantage, though: the knight is exposed to pawn moves, ...d5 hits the bishop and unmasks the c8-bishop against the knight, and Black gets time and the centre.

Trades the bishop for the knight, but after ...Rxg8 the queen still attacks g2 and White has to defend with the king in the centre and the pieces undeveloped. White has spent the bishop to hand Black a tempo, and Black has the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5.name: Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack, Poisoned Pawn Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5.background: Part of what is perhaps the most notorious and heavily analysed line of the Latvian Gambit.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Bc4 fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5.strategy: Takes the pawn and escapes the bishop's attack in one move, with the queen now hitting the rook on h1. The pawn is poisoned: White gets a strong check and an attack for sacrificed material, so Black must find a string of precise defensive moves.

Steps out of the bishop's attack and still hits the knight, but d4 guards it and the queen walks into Bf7+: after ...Qxf7 Nxf7 Kxf7 Qh5+ White wins the queen for a bishop and a knight and keeps an attack on the exposed king. The counterplay against g2 is gone for nothing.
Captures en passant but ignores the threat: the bishop on c1 already attacks the queen, and Bxg5 wins it for nothing. The pawn on d3 is no compensation.
Escapes the fork with tempo by taking g2 and hitting the rook on h1. White cannot cash in on h8, because the queen then takes the rook on h1 with check, so Black wins time and gets the initiative.
Steps out of the fork and hits the knight, but the bishop guards f7, so White takes the rook on h8. Black has little to show for it: no pawn on g2 won and no attack on the rook on h1.
Also escapes the fork and hits the knight and f2, but the bishop guards f7 and the king guards f2, so White takes the rook on h8 for free. Black passes up ...Qxg2 and its attack on the rook on h1.

The only move that saves the rook: it leaves the queen's attack for a square guarded by king and bishop, and the knight on f7 keeps its threat on h8. The price is time, with the king still in the centre and Black free to bring pieces into the attack.
Takes the rook, but ...Qxh1+ takes the other one with check. When the queens come off, the knight is stranded in the corner and White is a pawn down, so taking the rook is not as good as it looks.
Walks into ...Qf3+, which drives the king back to the first rank and then the queen takes the rook on h1. The king gains nothing on e2 and White loses the rook for no return.
Opens the c8-bishop, hits the bishop on c4 and prepares ...Bg4 against the queen. White can take the rook on h8, but then has to avoid being mated while the knight is far from the king.

Brings the knight into the attack, covers h5 and supports the pawn on e4. It is slower than opening the c8-bishop with a pawn move, so the attack takes longer to build against a king that is still short of cover: playable but risky.

Adds a piece to the attack and eyes d4 and b4, but leaves the c8-bishop and the d-pawn at home. It is playable but risky, as any move that does not open the bishop and hit the c4-bishop lets the attack run out of fuel.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6.strategy: A good and popular reply: it hits the knight and covers g6, so Qh5+ g6 stops being a threat. White keeps the extra pawn for now, and the early queen move costs Black time, but Black hopes to regain the pawn on e4 with an active game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6.strategy: The accurate answer: the knight guards h5, so Qh5+ disappears and with it White's strongest idea. Black stays a pawn down and leaves the knight alone, but develops safely and gives White the choice between keeping the pawn and returning it for development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nc6.name: Latvian Gambit: Fraser Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the knight and invites Qh5+ in the hope of winning time against the queen, but the plan fails: White takes on g6, then the bishop on f8, and comes out a clear exchange ahead. White can also just build a centre and keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qe7.name: Latvian Gambit: Greco Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qe7.strategy: Hits the knight, but leaves the king on the h5 diagonal: Qh5+ g6 Nxg6 forks queen and rook. Black's queen escapes with check and picks up the e4 pawn, but White ends up the exchange ahead and keeps the better game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6 4.Bc4.strategy: Offers the pawn back for development: the bishop and the knight on e5 aim at f7, and the natural recapture ...Nxe4 allows Qh5+ again, since the knight no longer guards h5. White returns the extra pawn for a lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6 4.exf5.strategy: Takes the f-pawn, but Black's ...Qe7 hits the knight and ...Bxf5 soon wins the pawn back, leaving White one pawn up in a quiet game. Sound enough, but it gives up the lead in development that Bc4 offers.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Builds a centre and supports the knight on e5, but it is too slow: with the knight on f6 guarding h5 there is no Qh5+ to punish ...fxe4, so Black wins the pawn back at once and the game is level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6 4.Bc4 fxe4.strategy: Takes back the pawn but walks into a position where knight and bishop strike at f7: Nf7 forks queen and rook. Black hopes to trap the knight that takes on h8 and attack the king, but accurate play leaves Black down material.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6 4.Bc4 d5.strategy: Blocks the bishop's diagonal and hits the bishop, so the fork and the check lose their sting, but it costs a pawn: White takes on d5 and Black has only quick development to show for it. The compensation falls short.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Nf6 4.Bc4 Qe7.strategy: The accurate defence: the queen leaves the fork square, hits the knight on e5 and guards f7, so the fork on d8 and h8 is gone. Black is still a pawn down and behind in development, but the position is sound and the knight can be challenged next.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Foltys-Leonhardt Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4.background: Recommended by Grandmaster Tony Kosten and now considered a more critical test of the gambit than 4.d4; its popularity has grown in recent years.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4.strategy: A respected alternative: the knight steps aside without blocking the d-pawn, so White can meet ...fxe4 with d3. It gives the extra pawn back at once, though, and keeps a smaller edge than the full centre of d4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Main Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4.background: The traditional main line of the Latvian Gambit; in recent years 4.Nc4 has gained in popularity.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4.strategy: Builds a full pawn centre and defends the knight on e5, so the pieces can develop freely. Black can only shift the knight with a pawn move that shuts in the f8-bishop, and White plays to keep the centre and the extra pawn while Black looks for activity.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nf3.strategy: Retreats to a square the pawn takes away: ...fxe4 attacks the knight again, and every square but g1 is covered by the queen on f6. White loses the extra pawn and several tempi, and Black gets the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6.strategy: Challenges the knight with a pawn, the way to make White decide, but it closes in the f8-bishop, and Black is a pawn behind. The idea is to take on e4 next and open lines for the queen and the other pieces.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and cramps White, but the knight on e5 stays put. Bc4 then aims at f7, where the knight would hit the rook on h8, and the king is stuck in the centre on the open e8-h5 diagonal, so White develops with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and on the knight, and gets a piece out before settling the pawn structure. Sound, but it does not change the balance: Black is still a pawn down and White defends the centre with a developing move and keeps the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Bilguer Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.strategy: Retreats the knight to a safe, active square. The e4 pawn is left undefended: White lets Black take it and relies on the centre and development, which tests whether the early queen sortie really helps Black.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nf.strategy: Retreats to f3, where ...fxe4 hits the knight at once and it must move again. Black regains the pawn with tempo, and White has lost the extra pawn and time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Ng.strategy: Hangs the knight: it attacks the queen on f6, but ...fxg4 takes it with the pawn. White has no compensation for the piece, and the tempo gained on the queen was an illusion.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.strategy: Black's long-planned capture. It restores material equality and puts a pawn on e4 that cramps White. The price is the open king: the e8-h5 diagonal is weak, so White develops with tempo against it.

Develops a piece and hits d4, a sound way to continue, but it leaves the pawn on e4 alone: White can take on f5 or develop, and Black must still win the pawn back. Taking on e4 at once regains it and cramps White, the more direct use of the move.

Challenges the knight on c4 with a developing move, but leaves the pawn on e4 alone. White can take on f5 or simply develop, and a bishop trade on c4 does not repay the pawn. Sound, but ...fxe4 first is more direct.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Bronstein Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, but does nothing about the pawn on e4. Black keeps it and gets time to consolidate, so White's chance to hit the exposed king with tempo is gone.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Nimzowitsch Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc.strategy: Brings the knight to e3, where it covers d5, f5 and g4. But it leaves the pawn on e4 alone and blocks the c1-bishop, so Black keeps the pawn, develops in peace and White's lead in development fades.

Provokes ...g6 but gains nothing: the queen is attacked and must retreat, and d4 loses its protection, so the queen on f6 hits it. White has spent two moves to weaken Black's kingside slightly and lost the lead in development.

Develops the knight with an attack on the e4 pawn: if Black ignores it, Nxe4 wins the pawn with tempo against the queen. The queen must defend and give up the pressure on d4, while White's pieces come out with gain of time.
The natural answer: the pawn attacks the queen with gain of tempo, and White must retreat while Black's queen eyes d4. The move slightly loosens the kingside but takes no risk.

Offers the queens: if White takes, the h-pawn recaptures. Black's pawns are doubled, but the h-file opens for the rook and the exposed king is relieved of the queen. It is the quieter way, but White keeps the better development.

Offers the queens on f7. After Qxf7+ Kxf7 the king is stuck in the centre and cannot castle, and White's lead in development remains. Black avoids the weakening pawn move but pays more for it than that move would cost.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 fxe4.strategy: Black captures at once, because waiting lets White take on f5 and keep the extra pawn. It also threatens ...d5, hitting the knight with a developing move, and leaves White to find the right way to contest the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 d5.strategy: Hits the knight at once, but White takes: exd5 wins a second pawn, and the queen's checks on the open e-file win nothing back. Black has given up the pawn that fxe4 would have recovered and has nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece but leaves the pawn on e4 to White: taking on f5 keeps the extra pawn even after the queen recaptures. Black has spent the move on development and has not yet won the pawn back.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 fxe4 5.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Leonhardt Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 fxe4 5.strategy: Hits the pawn on e4 with a developing move and covers d5, so the freeing ...d5 is not available. Material is level, but White has the better development and the safer king, and Black must now look after the pawn on e4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 fxe4 5.name: Latvian Gambit Accepted: Foltys Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nxe5 Qf6 4.Nc4 fxe4 5.strategy: Challenges the pawn on e4 at once, but ...d5 hits the knight on c4 with tempo and supports the e4 pawn. White's lead in development disappears and the game is level.

Steps out of the pawn's reach and covers d5, so ...d5 would simply lose a pawn. But the knight does nothing about the pawn on e4 and blocks the c1-bishop, so Black can bring the pieces out in peace with material level.
